objective: By the end of this lesson you can prove an airplane is legal and ready for IFR: check its inspections and required equipment, run the instrument checks from walk-around to takeoff roll, do and log a VOR check, confirm your database and charts are current, and handle inoperative equipment the legal way.
why: In the clouds you have nothing but the instruments. A bad gyro, a blocked static port or an expired database found on the ground is an easy fix; found in IMC it can be an emergency.

prereading.label: IFH 5-2 to 5-3

prereading.what: VOR accuracy, VOR receiver accuracy checks, VOT and certified checkpoints.
prereading.label: IFH 9-16 to 9-17

prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.171

prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.213

warmup: You are about to file IFR in a rental airplane you have not flown in a month. Before you even start the engine, what three things would you want to know about the airplane's paperwork and avionics?

key_terms.def: A step-by-step check of every flight instrument and its power source, done before any flight by instrument reference.
The pitot tube and static ports that feed the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI.
A valve, usually inside the flight deck, that gives the instruments static air if the outside static ports block.
A ground test signal for checking a VOR receiver. Centered CDI should show 0° FROM or 180° TO.
A certified radial you should receive at a marked spot on the airport or over a landmark in the air.
Card near the compass that shows what compass heading to steer for each magnetic heading.
A legally enforceable FAA rule that fixes an unsafe condition in an aircraft, engine, propeller or appliance.
An FAA-approved list, with a letter of authorization, that lets a specific aircraft fly with certain items inoperative.
Kinds of Operations Equipment List: shows which equipment is needed for VFR, IFR, day or night in that airplane.
A label next to the switch, control or indicator of an item that does not work, so no one relies on it.
FAA permission to fly an aircraft that does not meet airworthiness rules but can fly safely, usually to a repair shop.
The waypoints, airways and procedures stored in a GPS or FMS. It is updated every 28 days.

chunks.title: Why check the instruments before IFR?

body.p: The instrument check takes only a small part of your preflight time, but its importance cannot be overstated. Before any flight by instrument reference, check all instruments and their sources of power for proper operation [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

The law puts this on you. The pilot in command decides whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight, and must stop the flight if an unairworthy mechanical, electrical or structural condition occurs [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]].

head: Phase
What you are looking for
rows: Antennas, pitot tube and static ports clear; records; charts; instruments at rest read right [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]
Gyros spin up quietly, power source is good, compass and heading indicator agree, altimeter and VSI read right [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Turn coordinator, heading indicator and attitude indicator behave correctly in turns and straight taxi [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]

body.p: Checking the directional instruments before taxi also fights runway incursions. Good heading information keeps you sure where you are on the airport [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

callout.text: Use the checklist. It is a memory aid that keeps critical items from being forgotten. Pilots who don't take checklists seriously become complacent and rely on memory [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

body.p: The IFH steps are for conventional (round-dial) instruments. Airplanes with electronic flight displays use the procedures in their flight manual [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

check.q: Who decides if the airplane is in condition for safe flight?

body.p: No one may fly a civil aircraft unless it is airworthy [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(a)]]. It must carry a current airworthiness certificate and a registration certificate [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]], and you must follow the flight manual limits, markings and placards [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]].
Then check the logbooks. IFR adds several items to the VFR list:

head: Item
Interval
Rule
rows: Within the preceding 100 hours, if carrying people for hire or giving flight instruction for hire in an airplane the instructor provides
Altimeter, static system and altitude encoder test
Within the preceding 24 calendar months, to fly IFR in controlled airspace
Within 12 calendar months after the last one
VOR check (if you use VOR under IFR)

callout.text: 30 days: VOR. 12 months: annual and ELT. 24 months: altimeter/static and transponder. 100 hours: only when for hire.

body.p: The 100-hour limit may be passed by up to 10 hours only while flying to a place where the inspection can be done. That extra time counts toward the next 100 hours [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

ELT batteries must be replaced after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50% of their useful life has expired [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]. The IFH preflight also has you check the ELT battery replacement date and the 24-month altimeter and static check in the records [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

The owner or operator is primarily responsible for keeping the aircraft airworthy, including ADs [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. But anyone who operates a product that does not meet an AD is in violation, every time they fly it [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7 and 39.9]].

callout.text: No one may fly IFR in controlled airspace above the highest altitude at which the altimeters and altitude reporting system were tested [[60:525|14 CFR 91.411(d)]].

check.q: The altimeter and static system check was done 25 months ago. Can you file IFR in controlled airspace?
check.a: No. It must be within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]].

body.p: For IFR you need everything required for day VFR, plus night VFR equipment at night [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(1)]]. Then add these items, and all of them must work [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(a)]]:

head: 91.205(d) item
What it means in a typical trainer
rows: Two-way radio communication and navigation equipment suitable for the route
COM radio, plus VOR or IFR GPS that fits the route you fly [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(2)]]
Turn coordinator or turn-and-slip indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(3)]]
Sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure
Altimeter with a Kollsman window [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(5)]]
Clock showing hours, minutes and seconds
Sweep-second hand or digital clock [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(6)]]
Generator or alternator of adequate capacity

body.p: The day VFR basics still apply, such as airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic compass, tachometer, oil pressure and temperature, and fuel gauges [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]]. DME or a suitable RNAV system is only added at and above FL 240 [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(e)]].

Your airplane may also have a Kinds of Operations Equipment List (KOEL). It shows the equipment needed for VFR, IFR, day or night. Equipment the KOEL requires for IFR cannot be deferred for an IFR flight [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]].

callout.text: Under IFR, portable electronic devices are not allowed unless the operator of the aircraft has determined they will not interfere with its navigation or communication systems (voice recorders, hearing aids, pacemakers and shavers are exempt) [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]] [[43:1|AC 91.21-1D 1]].

check.q: Name two IFR items from 91.205(d) that are not required for day VFR.
check.a: Any two of: rate-of-turn indicator, slip-skid indicator, sensitive altimeter, clock with seconds, adequate generator or alternator, attitude indicator, heading indicator, radios suitable for the route [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]].

body.p: Errors in the airspeed indicator and VSI almost always mean a blocked pitot tube, static port, or both. Moisture, ice, dirt or insects can cause it. So on the walk-around, make sure the pitot cover is off and the static ports are clear and undamaged [[23:97|IFH 5-2]].
A blocked pitot tube affects only the airspeed indicator. A blocked static port affects the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

head: Before engine start
Check
rows: Antennas in good condition. Pitot cover off, pitot tube clear. Static ports clear, nothing near them that would disturb the airflow [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]
Altimeter and static check within 24 calendar months. ELT battery date [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]
Chart Supplement (the IFH still calls it the A/FD) and NOTAMs for the navaids you will use. Charts and handbooks right for departure, en route, destination and alternate [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]
Set the current altimeter setting. Pointers should show airport elevation [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Miniature aircraft level, ball about centered on level ground [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Full of fluid. Correction card in place and current [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Set to the correct time and running [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Alternate static valve, pitot heat, deice
Alternate static can open and is fully closed. Pitot heat works (watch the ammeter). Deice fluid quantity [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]

callout.text: Know where the alternate static source is before you need it. Using it, the altimeter reads slightly high, the airspeed reads high, and the VSI shows a brief climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

check.q: Which instruments go wrong if the static port is blocked?

chunks.title: After engine start: gyros, compass, altimeter and VSI

body.p: When you turn on the master switch, listen to the gyros spin up. Any hesitation or unusual noise should be checked before flight [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Then check their power source: the suction gauge for vacuum gyros, or the generators and inverters for electric gyros [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

A typical vacuum reading is 4.8 to 5.2 inches of mercury at 2,000 rpm, but use your POH values. A hasty taxi and run-up does not give mechanical gyros time to reach speed, and departing into IMC that way is unadvisable [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

head: Instrument
After-start check
rows: Card moves freely, bowl full. Compare with a known heading (runway heading) while stopped or taxiing straight. Note the card correction for the takeoff runway [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Allow 5 minutes for the gyro to spin up. Before or during straight taxi, set it to the compass. Check a slaved system for slaving [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
After spin-up, the horizon bar comes level and stays at the right attitude. A little vibration that slowly stops is normal [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
With the current setting, compare with known field elevation. Must be within 75 ft [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Should read zero. If not, tap the panel gently [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
Proper readings; radios working and set; deice working [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]

callout.text: Altimeter more than 75 ft off field elevation? Its accuracy is questionable and it should go to a repair station. The ramp can be higher or lower than field elevation, so recheck in the run-up area first [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. No altimeter setting available? Set field elevation [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

body.p: If the VSI can't be zeroed, use its ground reading as your zero mark [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]. In flight, remember the error. A VSI that shows 100 fpm down in level flight just means any change from that reading is a pitch change [[23:139|IFH 6-6]].
The compass correction card tells you what to steer. On this card, to fly magnetic 120° with the radios on, you steer 123° [[23:108|IFH 5-13]].

check.q: Field elevation is 1,135 ft. With the current altimeter setting the altimeter reads 1,180 ft. OK?
check.a: Yes. It is 45 ft off, within 75 ft [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

body.p: Taxiing is your best test bench. The airplane turns left and right, and you can watch every directional instrument respond [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

head: Instrument
Good
Bad
rows: Shows the direction of each taxi turn. Ball moves freely, opposite the turn. Level in straight taxi [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]
No turn shown, wrong direction, or a stuck ball
Shows the taxiway or runway direction when lined up, within 5° [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]
Turns the wrong way or drifts fast [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]
Horizon bar stays level in straight taxi and tips 5° or less in turns [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]
Tips more than 5° in taxi turns or won't stay level: unreliable [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]
Reads zero before takeoff, then rises at an appropriate rate on the takeoff roll [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]
No movement, or slow rise on the roll

body.p: At idle, vacuum gyros may not be at full speed, so precession can be faster than in flight [[1:224|PHAK 8-22]]. A strong wind into the pitot tube can make the airspeed read above zero on the ground [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

Adjust the miniature aircraft on the attitude indicator to the horizon bar on the ground. In some tricycle-gear airplanes, a slightly nose-low ground attitude gives level flight at cruise [[23:133|IFH 5-38]].

callout.text: At the run-up, recheck and set the flight instruments for departure, confirm the heading indicator agrees with the compass, set the heading bug, and set the avionics: frequencies, nav sources, courses, autopilot preselects and transponder code [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

check.q: In a left taxi turn, which way should the ball move?
check.a: To the right, opposite the turn, while the turn coordinator shows a left turn [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

body.p: To use VOR under IFR, the VOR equipment must be maintained under an approved procedure, or operationally checked within the preceding 30 days and found within limits [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

head: Method
How
Limit
rows: At the departure airport. Center the CDI: OBS reads 0° FROM or 180° TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4b]]
At a marked spot on the departure airport surface [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(2)]]
Only if no test signal or ground checkpoint is available [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]]
Pick a radial on an airway centerline and a prominent ground point, preferably more than 20 NM out. Fly over it at a reasonably low altitude [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)]]
Both tuned to the same station; compare bearings to it [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]]

body.p: A ground checkpoint is a painted circle with an arrow pointing toward the facility. Its sign gives the VOR, the check course and DME, black on yellow [[33:156|AIM 2-3-19]] [[33:157|AIM 2-3-20]]. Find VOTs and checkpoints in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4f]]. An RMI tuned to a VOT shows 180° on any OBS setting [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4b]].

callout.text: Log it: date, place, bearing error, and your signature, in the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. A repair-station signal also needs their entry certifying the bearing and date [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

body.p: Don't apply any correction except the manufacturer's correction card figures [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4f]]. Some rpm settings can make the CDI swing as much as ±6°; a small rpm change usually smooths it [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. Never use a VOR reading taken while you are transmitting [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

You can also check sensitivity: turn the OBS until the CDI moves from center to the last dot. It should take no more than 10° or 12° each side [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. The AIM recommends a yearly receiver calibration by a repair facility, because a weak receiver can look fine close to a VOT and fail far from the station [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4c]].

check.q: Tuned to a VOT with the CDI centered, your OBS reads 183° TO. Pass?

body.p: Before every flight you must become familiar with all available information about it; for IFR that includes weather, fuel, alternatives and known ATC delays [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]]. Your charts, handbooks and flight log must fit the departure, en route, destination and alternate airports [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

Navigation databases are updated every 28 days [[23:30|IFH 1-11]]. For IFR, the onboard navigation data must be current and appropriate for the region you fly [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)]]. Databases must be updated for IFR operations [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2)]].

head: When
Database check (AIM 1-1-17)
rows: Find the issue date and make sure your planned use is before the expiration date and time [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]]
Check that the provider has not published a notice limiting a waypoint or procedure [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]]
Review GPS NOTAMs and aeronautical information [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(a)(6)]]
Waypoint names match the chart exactly, and they are in a logical place and order [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)(b)]]

body.p: Approaches must be loaded by name from the current database, never typed in as waypoints [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(3)]]. Do not fly a GPS approach unless the procedure in the database is current [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]]. The AIM table of GPS uses notes that an expired database requires you to verify the data for en route and terminal use, and that an approach needs a current database or proof the procedure has not changed since it expired [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]].

callout.text: Check the amendment date on the chart, such as "Amdt 4 14Jan10". If the chart was amended on or after your database's expiration date, you must not use the database for that procedure [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3a Note 4]].

body.p: You, the end user, are ultimately responsible for making sure the database is current, including error notices from the avionics maker or data supplier [[29:264|IPH 6-14]]. An EFB can replace paper only if its navigation information is current, up to date and valid, as you verify [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]].

check.q: Name the two preflight database checks the AIM lists.
check.a: Planned use is before the expiration date and time, and no provider notice limits the waypoint or procedure [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]].

body.p: Under 14 CFR, all installed instruments and equipment must work before each departure, unless a rule gives relief [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. When you find an inoperative item on preflight, you have three choices: cancel, get maintenance, or legally defer it [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].
**No MEL (most single-engine trainers).** A non-turbine airplane may take off with an inoperative item only if all of the 91.213(d) conditions are met [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]:

bullets: 1. The item is NOT part of the VFR-day type certification equipment [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(i)]].
2. It is NOT shown as required on the equipment list or the KOEL for this kind of flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)]].
3. It is NOT required by 91.205 or any other Part 91 rule for this flight. For IFR, that includes all of 91.205(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].
4. It is NOT required by an airworthiness directive [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iv)]].
5. It is removed (control placarded, maintenance recorded) or deactivated and placarded "Inoperative" [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].
6. A certificated, appropriately rated pilot or maintenance person decides it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

body.p: Deactivation can be more than turning a switch off, because the switch may not remove power. It may mean pulling and securing the circuit breaker or removing the item. AC 91-67A says deactivation is not preventive maintenance: an authorized person does it and makes the maintenance record entry, and you may not fly without that entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. Place the placard next to the control or indicator, where the crew can see it [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.3]].

**With an MEL.** An approved MEL plus a letter of authorization (LOA) acts as a supplemental type certificate for that airplane [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]]. Once an LOA is issued, using the MEL becomes mandatory for that airplane [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. The MEL and LOA must be accessible to you; a phone call is not acceptable [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1]]. Some items can never go on an MEL, such as equipment required by an AD or by a Part 91 rule for the operation [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(b)]].

head: Situation
What you do
rows: Item can't be deferred and no repair is available
Special flight permit to fly it to a repair place [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]] [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]
Use the POH/AFM procedures. Deferral is not for in-flight discrepancies [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Before the next takeoff it must be fixed or deferred [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.3]]
Repaired, replaced, removed or inspected at the next required inspection [[60:521|14 CFR 91.405(c)]]
GPS fails before an IFR flight
Advise ATC and amend the equipment suffix on the flight plan [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(a)(5)]]

callout.text: An MEL never lets you break an operating rule. It only covers the airworthiness side [[58:8|AC 91-67A 1.7.2]]. Legal to defer does not mean wise to fly: think about the weather, night, airports, workload and other inoperative items [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]].

check.q: Your trainer has no MEL. The attitude indicator is inoperative. Can you defer it under 91.213(d) for an IFR flight?
check.a: No. It is required by 91.205(d)(8) for IFR, so 91.213(d)(2)(iii) bars the deferral [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]] [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the instrument flight deck check

body.p: Use the checklist for your airplane. The POH preflight section gives a systematic method [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Fit these IFR items into it:

bullets: 1. **Paperwork.** Airworthiness and registration certificates aboard [[60:485|14 CFR 91.203(a)]]. Annual, ADs, 24-month altimeter/static and transponder, ELT, VOR check within 30 days [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]] [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171]]. Any inoperative items placarded and recorded [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].
2. **Publications.** Current charts and database. NOTAMs and Chart Supplement for the navaids you'll use [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]].
3. **Walk-around.** Antennas, pitot tube, static ports [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].

4. **Before start.** Altimeter set to field elevation, VSI zero, turn coordinator level, compass full with a current card, clock running, alternate static closed, pitot heat works [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
5. **After start.** Gyros spin up quietly, suction or electrical source normal, compass vs. runway heading, wait 5 minutes and set the heading indicator, altimeter within 75 ft [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
6. **VOR check** at a VOT or ground checkpoint, and log it [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].
7. **Taxi.** Turn coordinator and ball, heading indicator, attitude indicator within 5° in turns [[23:132|IFH 5-37]] [[23:133|IFH 5-38]].
8. **Run-up.** Vacuum in range, instruments and avionics set for departure, takeoff briefing out loud [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].
9. **Takeoff roll.** Airspeed rising at an appropriate rate [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
10. **Decide.** Anything not right? Is it required for IFR? If yes, don't go IFR until it's fixed [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

head: ACS Skill
Standard
rows: Follow the checklist for the airplane and decide whether it is in condition for safe instrument flight (ACS IR.II.C.S1)

callout.text: Do the check out loud and point at each instrument. An examiner wants to hear what a good indication looks like and what you would do with a bad one.

check.q: When do you set the heading indicator to the compass?
check.a: About 5 minutes after start, before taxi or while taxiing straight [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

chunks.title: Risk: inoperative equipment and outdated data

body.p: Use PAVE to sort the hazards. Equipment problems belong to the Aircraft ("A") part [[30:11|RMH 1-2]].

**Inoperative equipment.** Any inoperative item is an "A" hazard. Example: a landing light is not required for Part 91 flights not for hire, but it may make a night operation more hazardous [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Ask how the item matters in the conditions you expect [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].
Redundancy matters more in IMC. One radio on a day VFR flight is not a big concern. One radio in IMC could be an "A" hazard, and instrument failure is a concern in IMC or at night [[30:24|RMH 3-6]].

The RMH example: a vacuum pump failed in VMC, taking out the attitude and heading indicators. The pilot continued into IMC instead of landing, which stacked an "A" hazard on a "V" (environment) hazard [[30:11|RMH 1-2]].

bullets: Before flying with a deferred item, weigh: hazard from the item and its failure, multiple failures together, weather, night, airports, en route area, diversion options, extra workload, fatigue [[58:25|AC 91-67A 4.4]].
Fix inoperative items at the earliest opportunity [[58:8|AC 91-67A 1.7.4]].
If a fault shows up during start or taxi, you must not take off until it is repaired or properly deferred [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1.2]].

body.p: **Outdated publications and databases.** An old database can hold wrong waypoints, frequencies or procedures. Pilots may not notice database errors, so constantly make sure the data is accurate and current, and be ready to go back to conventional navigation [[29:264|IPH 6-14]]. A database can even show an airport as usable when it is closed [[29:265|IPH 6-15]].

callout.text: Update the database before an IFR flight, not after you find a problem. If it will expire during the flight, plan how you will verify the data [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3a Note 4]].

check.q: In PAVE, which letter covers an inoperative landing light?
check.a: A, for aircraft. Inoperative equipment triggers an "A" hazard [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

bullets: Rushing the taxi and run-up so vacuum gyros never reach speed [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].
Setting the heading indicator before the gyro has had 5 minutes to spin up [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
Comparing the altimeter on a ramp that is not at field elevation and not rechecking in the run-up area [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
Leaving the pitot cover on or not looking at the static ports [[23:97|IFH 5-2]].
Doing the VOR check but not logging date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].
Reading the VOR while transmitting, or adding your own correction [[23:259|IFH 9-16]] [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4f]].
Not checking the database expiration date before an IFR flight [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]].
Pulling a breaker, taping on a note and calling it deferred, with no maintenance entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]].
Trying to defer an item 91.205(d) requires for IFR [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]].

check.q: Why recheck the altimeter in the run-up area?
check.a: The ramp may be at a different elevation than the field, so the error may be smaller there [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-1. A typical electrically heated pitot-static head.
f1.alt: Cutaway of a pitot-static head showing ram air entering the pitot tube past a baffle plate, drain holes, static holes, a static chamber, 100 watt and 35 watt heaters and a pitot heater switch. Red tubing carries pitot pressure to the airspeed indicator; blue tubing links a static port and an alternate static source to the airspeed indicator, VSI and altimeter.

f2.caption: Figure 5-19. A compass correction card shows the deviation correction for any heading.
f2.alt: Compass correction card with FOR headings 000 to 330 in 30 degree steps and STEER values with radios on and off; for example, for 120 steer 123 with radios on and 125 with radios off.

f3.caption: Figure 5-28. Single-engine instrument vacuum system using a steel-vane, wet-type vacuum pump.
f3.alt: Diagram of a vane-type vacuum pump drawing air through a central air filter, the heading indicator, attitude indicator and turn-and-slip indicator, with a suction gauge, needle valve, suction-relief valve and an oil separator venting air overboard.

f4.alt: Painted circle with a white outer ring and yellow inner ring around a black interior, holding a yellow arrow aligned toward the VOR facility; notes say the circle may have 6 inch black bands for contrast.

f5.alt: Three stacked boxes joined by arrows: Database Providers collect the data, format it per ARINC 424 and maintain it; Avionics Manufacturers decide what is included, how it is processed and the user interface; Pilots (End Users) ensure currency, execute updates and must know the avionics that use the database.

scenario.title: Early IFR departure in a club airplane
scenario.setup: You plan a 7 a.m. IFR flight in your flying club's single-engine airplane. The club has no MEL. Ceilings are 800 ft and the destination will be IMC. On preflight you find: the last VOR check in the log was 34 days ago; the GPS database expired yesterday; the landing light does not work; and on taxi the attitude indicator tips about 10° in each turn. Your passenger needs to make a 10 a.m. meeting.

questions.q: Can you use the VOR under IFR today?
questions.a: Not until you check it again. The check must be within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. Use a VOT or ground checkpoint at the airport (±4°) or compare dual VORs (4°), then log date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)-(d)]].

questions.q: What about the expired GPS database?
questions.a: Databases must be updated for IFR [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17b1(c)(2)]], and preflight you must confirm the planned use is before the expiration date [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]]. Update it. If you could not, the AIM table says en route and terminal data must be verified and approaches need a current database or proof the procedure has not changed [[33:101|AIM TBL 1-1-6]].

questions.q: The attitude indicator tips about 10° in taxi turns. What does that mean?
questions.a: It is unreliable; more than 5° in taxi turns fails the check [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. An attitude indicator is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]], so it cannot be deferred for this flight [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. No IFR flight until it is repaired.

questions.q: Could the landing light be deferred?
questions.a: Possibly. It is not required for Part 91 flights not for hire [[30:25|RMH 3-7]]. Under 91.213(d) it must not be on the equipment list or KOEL as required, it must be deactivated and placarded "Inoperative" with the maintenance entry, and a rated person must decide it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]] [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. Still weigh the risk of a night or low-ceiling arrival [[30:25|RMH 3-7]].

questions.q: Your passenger is pushing you to go. How do you handle it?
questions.a: That is an External pressure in PAVE. Ask why the flight is being made and whether the trip is worth the risks [[30:11|RMH 1-2]]. With a failed required instrument the answer is already set: you are responsible for airworthiness and must not fly it IFR [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7]].

skills.do: Perform the preflight inspection by following the checklist for your airplane, including the instrument checks before start, after start and during taxi, and decide whether the airplane is in condition for safe instrument flight (ACS IR.II.C.S1).
skills.practice: Run the IFH sequence with your POH checklist on every training flight, out loud [[23:131|IFH 5-36]] [[23:132|IFH 5-37]] [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. Make a one-page list of your airplane's inspection dates from its logbooks [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409]] [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411]], and do and log a VOR check at your home airport [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

quiz.q: Before engine start you set the altimeter to the current setting. It reads 110 ft above field elevation on the ramp. What should you do?
options: Recheck in the run-up area; if still more than 75 ft off, its accuracy is questionable
Nothing; up to 100 ft of error is allowed for IFR
Reset the altimeter setting until it shows field elevation and go
Switch to the alternate static source and recheck
quiz.why: More than 75 ft off makes the altimeter questionable and it should be referred to a repair station. The ramp may differ from field elevation, so recheck in the run-up area [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

quiz.q: Using a VOT, what is the maximum permissible bearing error?
quiz.why: A VOT or repair-station test signal allows ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. ±6° is for airborne checks.

quiz.q: Which item is NOT required by 14 CFR 91.205(d) for IFR below FL 240?
options: Slip-skid indicator
Clock with hours, minutes and seconds
DME
Generator or alternator of adequate capacity
quiz.why: DME or suitable RNAV is required only at and above FL 240 [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(e)]]. The others are in 91.205(d) [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]].

quiz.q: How often must the altimeter, static system and altitude encoder be tested to fly IFR in controlled airspace?
options: Every 12 calendar months
Every 100 hours
Every 30 days
Every 24 calendar months
quiz.why: Within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]].

quiz.q: During a right taxi turn, what should the turn coordinator and ball show?
options: Right turn; ball moves left
Right turn; ball moves right
Wings level; ball centered
Left turn; ball moves left
quiz.why: The turn instrument shows the direction of the turn, and the ball moves opposite the turn [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

quiz.q: Under 91.213(d), who may decide that an inoperative item is not a hazard?
options: Only an FAA inspector
Only the aircraft owner
A certificated, appropriately rated pilot or maintenance person
Any passenger with a pilot certificate
quiz.why: A pilot certificated and rated under Part 61, or a person rated to maintain the aircraft, makes the determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]].

quiz.q: Lined up on the runway, the heading indicator should agree with the runway direction within:
quiz.why: Recheck before takeoff: within 5° of the known runway or taxiway direction [[23:133|IFH 5-38]].

quiz.q: According to the AIM, what is the first preflight check of your GPS database?
options: Planned use is before the database expiration date and time
The database was loaded by a mechanic
The database holds every airport in the U.S.
Each waypoint's latitude and longitude matches the chart
quiz.why: Determine the issue date and verify that the date and time of use is before expiration [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(4)]]. Checking every lat/long is not required [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17 Note]].

quiz.q: Your VOR check used the airborne method over a prominent ground point on an airway. What is the maximum error?
quiz.why: The airway check in flight allows 6° between the published radial and the indicated bearing [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(b)(4)(iii)]].

takeaways: Before any IFR flight, check every instrument and its power source. You, the PIC, decide airworthiness.
Logbooks: annual 12 months, ELT 12 months, altimeter/static and transponder 24 months, VOR check 30 days, ADs complied with.
Altimeter within 75 ft of field elevation; heading indicator within 5° of the runway; attitude indicator tips 5° or less in taxi turns.
VOR check: VOT or ground checkpoint ±4°, airborne ±6°, dual VOR 4°. Log date, place, error, signature.
Keep the database current for IFR and check its expiration date before every flight.
No MEL: defer only items not required by type certificate, equipment list or KOEL, 91.205, or an AD; deactivate, placard and record. Anything 91.205(d) needs means no IFR.
cfi_notes: IFH 9-16 says the VOR check needs "an appropriate endorsement." The rule actually requires a log entry with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. Teach the CFR.
IFH 5-36 and 9-16 still say "A/FD." It is now the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4f]].

PHAK 9-10 says deactivation "may be as simple as the pilot positioning a circuit breaker to the OFF position." The newer AC 91-67A (10/16/23) says deactivation is not preventive maintenance and an authorized person must do it and make the 43.9 entry [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. Teach the AC and explain the difference.
AIM 1-1-17 says databases must be updated for IFR, while the notes to TBL 1-1-6 describe verifying expired data. Teach "current" as the standard and the table notes as the narrow exception.
Examiners commonly ask the applicant to find each inspection in the logbooks and to walk through 91.213(d) for an inoperative item. Have students practice both on the airplane they will use.
Students often set the heading indicator right after start. Have them time the 5-minute spin-up and watch the vacuum gauge during the run-up.
On a glass-panel airplane, use the AFM procedures for the PFD and the backup instruments, since the IFH steps are for conventional instruments [[23:131|IFH 5-36]].
gaps: Airplane-specific checklists, suction ranges and electronic flight display (PFD/AHRS) self-tests come from each POH/AFM; the IFH only says to consult the flight manual.
AC 91-67A Figure 4-1 (PIC Decision Sequence) is a graphic with no text in the source; the deferral steps here come from 14 CFR 91.213(d) and PHAK 9-9.
No FAA handbook has a common-errors list for this Task; the Common errors chunk is built from IFH, PHAK, AFH and AC 91-67A cautions.
How to view the database expiration date on a specific GPS or FMS is in the manufacturer's manual, which is not in these sources.
AC 91.21-1D is aimed mostly at operators; it gives no specific test for a pilot checking a tablet or phone for interference.

activities.title: How often is it due?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

activities.title: The IFH instrument check, in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Walk-around: antennas, pitot tube cover off, static ports clear
Records: altimeter and static check within 24 months, ELT battery date
Before start: set the altimeter and check it shows field elevation
Master on: listen to the gyros spin up
Wait 5 minutes, then set the heading indicator to the compass
Taxi turns: turn coordinator shows the turn, ball moves opposite
Lined up: heading indicator within 5° of runway heading
Takeoff roll: airspeed rising at an appropriate rate

activities.title: True or false: the VOR check
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: With a VOT tuned and the CDI centered, the OBS should read 0° with a FROM flag.
An airborne checkpoint may be used even when a ground checkpoint is available at the airport.
cards.why: No. Airborne checkpoints are for when neither a test signal nor a ground checkpoint is available [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]].

cards.s: With dual VORs, you may check one against the other; the limit is 4° between them.
cards.why: Yes, tuned to the same station [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

cards.s: After the check, an instructor's endorsement in your pilot logbook is what the rule requires.
cards.why: No. Enter the date, place and bearing error and sign the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

cards.s: It is fine to add your own correction to the VOR reading to bring it within limits.
cards.why: No. Only the manufacturer's correction card figures may be applied [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4f]].

cards.s: A VOR check is required within the preceding 30 days to use VOR under IFR, unless the equipment is maintained under an approved procedure.

activities.title: Inoperative equipment words
activities.intro: Tap a term, then tap its meaning.

pairs.r: Lets this one aircraft fly with listed items inoperative
Shows equipment needed for VFR, IFR, day or night
Label next to the item's switch or indicator
Lets an unairworthy but safe aircraft fly to repairs
Legally enforceable fix for an unsafe condition
Deferral path for non-turbine airplanes without an MEL

final_quiz.q: At the airport you tune the VOT. With the CDI centered, the OBS reads 175° with a TO flag. What do you conclude?
options: Within limits; a VOT allows ±6°
Out of limits; the error is 5° and the limit is ±4°
Within limits; the error is only 1°
You can't tell; a VOT only works with an RMI
final_quiz.why: A good receiver reads 180° TO, so 175° is a 5° error [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4b]]. The VOT limit is ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. Correct the error before IFR flight [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4f]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has two independent VORs tuned to the same station. VOR 1 shows a bearing of 093° to the station and VOR 2 shows 098°. Can you use this as your VOR check?
options: Yes; the limit for a dual check is 6°
Yes; each is within 4° of the average
No; you may never check one VOR against the other
No; they differ by 5° and the limit is 4°
final_quiz.why: The maximum permissible variation between the two bearings is 4°; 098 - 093 = 5° [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

final_quiz.q: Which entry meets the VOR check record rule?
options: "VOR checked OK" with your initials
Date, place, bearing error, and your signature
The VOR frequency and the time of day
An instructor's endorsement in your pilot logbook
final_quiz.why: Enter the date, place and bearing error and sign the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

final_quiz.q: Field elevation is 820 ft. With the current setting, the altimeter shows 920 ft on the ramp and 905 ft in the run-up area, which is at field elevation. What now?
options: Fine; the run-up reading is within 100 ft
Fine; use the ramp reading since that is where you set it
Questionable; it is 85 ft off and should go to a repair station
Questionable only if the VSI is also off
final_quiz.why: 905 - 820 = 85 ft, more than 75 ft, even after the run-up recheck. Its accuracy is questionable; refer it to a repair station [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

final_quiz.q: The transponder was tested 20 months ago. The altimeter and static system were tested 26 months ago. Can you fly IFR in Class E airspace?
options: No; the altimeter and static test is past 24 calendar months
Yes; only the transponder test matters for IFR
Yes; the static test is only needed above 18,000 ft
No; both tests are due every 12 months
final_quiz.why: IFR in controlled airspace needs the altimeter, static system and encoder tested within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)]]. The transponder test is 24 months too [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]].

final_quiz.q: Your no-MEL trainer has one inoperative item. Which one could you possibly defer under 91.213(d) for a Part 91 IFR flight not for hire?
options: The attitude indicator
The slip-skid indicator
The clock
The landing light
final_quiz.why: The attitude indicator, slip-skid indicator and clock are required by 91.205(d), so 91.213(d)(2)(iii) bars deferring them [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. A landing light is not required for Part 91 flights not for hire [[30:25|RMH 3-7]], if no other list requires it.

final_quiz.q: According to AC 91-67A, what is true about deactivating an inoperative item under 91.213(d)?
options: Turning off its switch is always enough
It is preventive maintenance any pilot may do
It may need more than a switch, and an authorized person must make the maintenance entry
It needs a written FAA approval for each item
final_quiz.why: A switch may not remove power, so deactivation may mean securing the breaker or removing the item. It is not preventive maintenance, and the 43.9 entry is required before flight [[58:24|AC 91-67A 4.2.2]]. No FAA application is needed for 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.1]].

final_quiz.q: Your flying club got an FAA letter of authorization for an MEL on its airplane. A position light fails before a flight. How must you handle it?
options: Use 91.213(d) because it is simpler
Follow the MEL; once the LOA is issued it is mandatory
Defer it by phone with the club's mechanic
Ignore it; position lights are never required
final_quiz.why: Once an LOA is issued, using the MEL becomes mandatory for that aircraft [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. The MEL and LOA must be accessible; a phone call is not acceptable [[58:27|AC 91-67A 5.1]].

final_quiz.q: Your GPS database expires Nov 5. The RNAV (GPS) approach chart you plan to fly shows "Amdt 2 06Nov". What does the AIM say?
options: Use it; the database is still in date today
Use it if RAIM is available
Use it after typing in the new waypoints by hand
Don't use the database for it; the amendment is on or after expiration
final_quiz.why: If the procedure amendment date is on or after the database expiration date, you must not use the database for that operation [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3a Note 4]]. Approaches may never be built from hand-entered waypoints [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17b2(b)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: The ELT was used for 1 hour 20 minutes during a search last month. What must happen to its batteries?
options: They must be replaced or recharged
Nothing until 50% of their life has passed
Nothing until the next annual
Only the transmitter needs a test
final_quiz.why: Batteries must be replaced or recharged when the transmitter has been used more than 1 cumulative hour [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: A flight school gives flight instruction for hire in its own airplane. That airplane is at 100.0 hours since its last 100-hour inspection. The shop is at another airport 1.2 hours away. What may you do?
options: Keep flying lessons for up to 10 more hours
Nothing; it can't fly at all
Fly it to the shop; the extra time counts toward the next 100 hours
Fly lessons until the annual is due
final_quiz.why: The 100-hour limit may be exceeded by up to 10 hours only while en route to a place where the inspection can be done, and that time counts toward the next 100 [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

final_quiz.q: In the run-up area the suction gauge reads 3.5 "Hg at 2,000 rpm. The POH range starts at 4.5. IMC is reported at departure. Best decision?
options: Go; the gyros will catch up in the climb
Don't depart into IMC; the gyros may not be driven properly
Go, but use the turn coordinator only
Go after resetting the heading indicator
final_quiz.why: The suction must suit the instruments [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Without adequate vacuum the gyros may not reach proper speed, and departing into IMC is unadvisable [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].

final_quiz.q: During taxi turns, the attitude indicator's horizon bar tips about 8°. What does this tell you?
options: Normal; gyros always tip in taxi turns
Normal if it stops vibrating after takeoff
Unreliable; more than 5° in taxi turns fails the check
Unreliable only if the heading indicator also drifts
final_quiz.why: If the horizon bar tips more than 5° during taxi turns, the instrument is unreliable [[23:133|IFH 5-38]]. It is required for IFR [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(8)]].
